summary: Number bonds to 10 for ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1): for any number 1-9, find the number that makes 10 when added to it (7→3, 6→4). The ten-frame is the key structure because the empty cells make the complement visible, moving children from counting-on to seeing/recalling the bond. Bonds should become a fact family linking addition and subtraction (7+3=10 ⇔ 10−7=3) and be built toward rapid both-directions recall, because they underpin the making-ten strategy, column carrying and mental calculation through KS1/KS2.
misconceptions: Counting on from the given number every time rather than recalling the bond, so speed never develops.
Knowing 7 + 3 = 10 but not the related 10 − 7 = 3 (bond not held as a fact family).
Confusing bonds to 10 with bonds to other totals when the ten-frame isn't present.
Thinking there is only one 'way to make 10' rather than a full set of pairs.
Miscounting the empty cells on the ten-frame, giving a complement off by one.

activities.title: Ten-frame 'make ten' practice
steps: Look at a ten-frame holding some counters (e.g. 7 counters, so 3 cells are empty).
Before counting, predict how many more counters are needed to make 10.
Add (drag, tap, or place physical counters) the missing counters to fill the frame to 10, then check.
Say and record the matching equation, e.g. 7 + 3 = 10.
Repeat with different starting numbers 1-9, working toward naming the complement without counting the empty cells one by one.
activities.insight: The empty cells of the ten-frame ARE the answer: once the ten-frame becomes a mental picture, the complement is recognised at a glance rather than counted up.

activities.title: Link each bond to its subtraction partner
steps: Start from a known bond shown on a ten-frame, e.g. 7 + 3 = 10.
Remove the added part (the 3) and state the matching subtraction fact: 10 − 3 = 7.
Also state the commutative partner, 3 + 7 = 10, and the other subtraction fact, 10 − 7 = 3 (take away the 7 to see the 3 that remains).
Write the full fact family for the pair.
Answer quick questions in both directions, e.g. '__ + 6 = 10' and '10 − 6 = __'.
activities.insight: Each pair that makes 10 is one fact family, not several separate facts: knowing 7+3 means you also know 3+7, 10−7 and 10−3.

activities.title: Work through the complete set systematically
steps: Notice the symmetry (each pair appears both ways around) and that 5+5 is the one pair of equal parts.
Use a partitioned ten-strand, a two-colour ten of beads, or one row of a rekenrek (ten beads grouped as five and five in two colours) to show the same pairs physically.
Keep a reference display of the full set and tap/reveal a partner for any starting number.
Tell the whole set from memory as it becomes secure.
activities.insight: There is a complete, finite set of ways to make 10 with its own symmetry — not just one 'way to make 10' and not an endless list.

activities.title: Short, fast retrieval practice for automaticity
steps: Answer quick-fire 'make ten' items with the frame gradually hidden, e.g. shown '7' respond '3'.
Fill in missing-number sentences such as '__ + 6 = 10' and include a related subtraction such as '10 − 2 = __'.
Match starting numbers to their partners that make 10.
Aim for quick answers from memory, returning to the ten-frame image whenever a bond is uncertain.
activities.insight: Frequent, low-stakes retrieval turns worked-out complements into instantly recalled facts.

activities.title: Talk-it-through quick-fire (oral reasoning)
steps: Answer spoken 'how many more to make 10?' questions for various starting numbers.
Explain how the ten-frame helped: 'I saw three empty cells.'
Answer a follow-up that checks the fact family: 'If 7 and 3 make 10, what do 3 and 7 make?'
activities.insight: Being able to say how you found the complement shows whether the child is seeing the structure or still counting.

checkQuestion: Here is a ten-frame with 7 counters in it. How many more counters do we need to make 10? Now clear it and put in 4 — how many more to make 10 this time?
checkAnswer: 3, then 6 — ideally read straight off the empty cells of the ten-frame or recalled as a known bond, not counted up one by one.
